name: Energy and renewables
summary: Ethiopia had 9,761 MW of installed generating capacity in 2025, more than 95% of it renewable, and targets up to 14,000 MW by 2030, including the 5,150 MW Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam. The government's National Energy Compact calls for at least US$3.06 billion of private investment in 2026 to 2030, with solar, wind and off-grid power open to independent power producers. Tariffs are being raised toward full cost recovery by 2028, and power exports to neighboring countries earned 366 million USD in the first nine months of the current fiscal year.

opportunities.title: Solar and wind IPPs
opportunities.detail: A 225 MW solar IPP/PPP is in procurement, and 802 MW of wind and 625 MW of solar are listed as unfunded projects seeking finance.

opportunities.title: Aysha I wind farm
opportunities.detail: The 300 MW Aisha 1 wind project has a signed PPA with AMEA and is awaiting financial close.

opportunities.title: Off-grid and last-mile access
opportunities.detail: About 9.23 million connections are targeted by 2030, leaving a gap of 6.25 million (about 1.25 million per year) beyond existing programs, with 30% of 2030 access planned off-grid.

opportunities.title: Regional power trade
opportunities.detail: Exports of about 1,500 GWh/year are targeted to exceed 5,000 GWh/year by 2030, with PPAs to be finalized with South Sudan and Somalia.

opportunities.title: Geothermal development
opportunities.detail: Geothermal potential is about 10 GW with less than 1% exploited, while the Aluto-Langano expansion, Corbetti and Tulu Moye projects have stalled.

incentives.detail: The Compact offers currency risk mitigation through MIGA and IDA guarantees, blended finance and results-based financing, standardized PPA models and an IPP helpdesk at the Ministry of Finance.

Investment Proclamation 1180/2020 encourages IPPs through long-term PPAs and standardized renewable auctions, and allows private investors to develop off-grid solar, small hydro, wind, biomass and hybrid systems.
The World Bank approved a US$400 million IDA credit plus a US$24 million Denmark grant for the ASCENT program, which seeks to incentivize private sector participation in electricity access.

risks.detail: Key risks named by the government and World Bank include IPP delays, payment risk, foreign exchange availability, non-cost-recovery tariffs, and hydrological risk.
Utility finances are weak: tariffs are below cost recovery, technical and commercial losses exceed 20%, and metering coverage is below 10%.
The World Bank-financed Aluto geothermal project confirmed 28.6 MW against 70 MW planned at appraisal and did not mobilize private capital.
